planting.note: Start seed indoors in a sterile, mineral cactus mix with bottom heat, or set out nursery transplants in spring into very well-drained, gravelly, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; this is one of the largest and slowest-growing barrel cacti, taking many decades to approach landscape-specimen size.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gravelly or sandy, lean soil in full sun; native to the Chihuahuan Desert and central Mexican highlands, this massive, solitary, ribbed barrel cactus slowly builds a dense crown of woolly, golden-brown spines and felted hair as it ages, eventually producing a ring of small yellow flowers atop older specimens in summer. Historically its sugar-rich flesh was harvested and candied as 'acitron' for Mexican sweets, a practice that depleted many wild populations and makes nursery-propagated stock the only responsible source for the trade. Growth from seed is extremely slow, so expect a small, rounded seedling for the first several years before it begins to resemble the classic barrel form; protect from prolonged freezes and winter wet, which cause rot far more readily than cold alone.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Start seed indoors in sterile, gritty cactus mix, or set out nursery-grown plants in spring into rocky, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; this slow-growing barrel is more tolerant of winter cold than most Mexican barrel cacti when kept bone-dry, but still fares best with overhead protection from freezing rain.

directions: Plant in rocky, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; native to the Chihuahuan Desert of West Texas, New Mexico, and northern Mexico, this solitary, strongly ribbed, blue-gray globular cactus is covered in stout, curved, pinkish-gray spines that curl distinctively around the ribs. Large, satiny pink to magenta-pink flowers open at the woolly crown in late spring and early summer, followed by small woolly fruit. It is slower-growing and more solitary than its relative the horse crippler (Echinocactus texensis), rarely offsetting, and needs essentially no supplemental water once established in sharply drained, rocky or caliche soil.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

common_name: Fire Barrel Cactus (San Pedro Martir Barrel Cactus)

planting.note: Start seed indoors in a sterile, mineral cactus mix, or set out nursery transplants in spring into very well-drained, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun; spine color intensifies with age and strong, direct sunlight.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gravelly or sandy, lean soil in full sun; native to the Baja California peninsula of Mexico, this solitary, columnar barrel cactus is prized above all for its densely packed, brilliant red to orange-red spines, which give the whole plant a glowing, fiery appearance that intensifies with maturity and sun exposure. Yellow flowers often flushed with red or orange open in a ring at the woolly crown in summer, followed by small yellow fruit. It is slower to establish than desert barrel cacti like Ferocactus wislizeni and benefits from being sited in a hot, reflective microclimate with excellent drainage, since it is more sensitive to cold, wet winter soil than many Sonoran Desert relatives.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Start seed indoors in a sterile, mineral cactus mix, or set out nursery transplants in spring into very well-drained, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun; this species is more cold-sensitive than desert barrel cacti native farther north and needs a warm, sheltered site outside the warmest zones.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gravelly or sandy, lean soil in full sun; native to coastal Sonora and Sinaloa, Mexico, this solitary, cylindrical barrel cactus carries broad, flattened, strongly hooked central spines banded in red and cream against dense yellow radial spines, giving mature plants a bold, patterned look. Orange to red-orange, funnel-shaped flowers open in a ring at the crown in summer, followed by yellow fruit. It is closely related to and sometimes confused in cultivation with Ferocactus wislizeni, but tends to be more cold-sensitive, reflecting its milder native coastal range, so give it the warmest, most sheltered position available outside of zone 10-11 gardens.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright, filtered light to morning sun in fast-draining cactus mix; like other Gymnocalycium species it tolerates and often prefers some protection from the most intense afternoon sun.

directions: Grow in very well-drained, gritty soil in bright, filtered light or morning sun with afternoon shade. Native to rocky hillsides in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, this dull grayish-green to olive globular cactus has broad, rounded ribs and short, curved spines, and is best known for producing unusually large, satiny, deep rose-pink flowers relative to its body size, among the showiest blooms in the genus. It flowers readily even on young plants in late spring and summer and slowly offsets with age to form a small cluster. Keep nearly dry through winter and resume watering gradually as new growth and flower buds appear in spring.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference
San Diego Cactus and Succulent Society

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; dense golden spination develops best with strong, direct light.

directions: Grow in very well-drained, gritty soil in bright light to full sun. Native to Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, and long sold in the succulent trade under its older name Notocactus buiningii, this small, solitary to sparingly offsetting globular cactus is densely clothed in fine, glossy, golden-yellow spines that nearly obscure the green body beneath. Bright yellow, cup-shaped flowers open at the crown in summer, often covering the top of the plant when several buds open together. Water only when the soil is fully dry and keep nearly dry through a cool winter rest to encourage the following summer's bloom.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; a cool, dry winter rest improves spring and summer flowering.

directions: Grow in very well-drained, gritty soil in bright light to full sun. Native to grassland hillsides in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, this small, flattened-globular cactus carries comb-like rows of fine, silvery-white radial spines pressed close against a gray-green body, giving it a frosted appearance. Pale yellow flowers with a reddish throat open at the crown in summer and are followed by small woolly fruit. It stays compact for years, rarely exceeding a few inches across, and suits a shallow pot or rock-garden pocket alongside other small South American globular cacti.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Let a harvested pad callus for one to two weeks in a dry, shaded spot, then set the cut end into very well-drained, sandy or rocky, alkaline soil in full sun in spring.

directions: Plant callused pads in very well-drained, sandy or rocky, alkaline soil in full sun. Native to the dry highlands of central Mexico, this tree-forming prickly pear is grown for its enormous, nearly circular, powdery blue-gray pads that can reach a foot across, held on a thickening woody trunk with age and armed with sparse, pale yellow spines. Bright yellow flowers appear along the pad margins in late spring, followed by sweet, deep reddish-purple fruit. It is notably cold-tolerant for a tree-forming Opuntia and spreads readily from rooted pads, but in mild, wet climates outside its native range it has naturalized aggressively and is regulated as a weed in parts of Australia and South Africa, so site and maintain it as a deliberate landscape specimen rather than letting dropped pads root unchecked.

planting.note: Let a harvested pad callus for one to two weeks in a dry, shaded spot, then set the cut end into very well-drained, sandy soil in full sun in spring; this tree-forming species takes many years to develop a true woody trunk.

directions: Plant callused pads in very well-drained, sandy soil in full sun. Native to central and northern Mexico, this large, tree-forming prickly pear eventually develops a thick woody trunk topped with a broad crown of rounded pads that are covered, especially on new growth, in long, shaggy, white hair-like spines that give the whole plant a pale, frosted look from a distance. Yellow flowers appear along the pad edges in spring, followed by sweet, juicy, deep red-purple fruit that is a traditional market crop in Mexico, and the young pads (nopalitos) are also harvested as a vegetable. It is slower to form a trunk in cultivation than in its native range and is more cold-sensitive than hardier prickly pears, so it is best suited to low-desert and coastal landscapes rather than regions with hard freezes.

planting.note: Let a harvested pad callus for one to two weeks in a dry, shaded spot, then set the cut end into very well-drained, rocky or sandy soil in full sun in spring; established plants develop a single woody trunk over many years.

directions: Plant callused pads in very well-drained, rocky or sandy soil in full sun. Native to rocky slopes of the Mojave and Sonoran Deserts in Arizona, California, Nevada, Utah, and northern Mexico, this tree-forming prickly pear grows a single trunk topped by a rounded, almost umbrella-shaped canopy of nearly circular, blue-green to gray-green pads armed with golden-brown spines. Pale yellow flowers tinged red open along the upper pad edges in late spring, followed by dry, spiny, dull purple fruit that is less palatable than that of many other prickly pears. It is among the more cold-hardy tree-forming Opuntia species, tolerating the cooler winters of higher desert elevations better than Mexican lowland species like O. leucotricha.

planting.note: Let a cut section callus for one to two weeks in a dry, shaded spot, then set the base an inch or two into very well-drained, sandy soil in full sun in spring; growth is fast for a columnar cactus under warm, well-fed conditions.

directions: Plant a callused cutting in very well-drained, sandy soil in full sun. Native to the semi-arid caatinga scrublands of northeastern Brazil, mandacaru is a fast-growing, tree-forming columnar cactus with thick, blue-green, strongly ribbed stems that branch upward from a short trunk, eventually reaching tree size in frost-free climates. Large, white, funnel-shaped flowers open at night in summer and are followed by egg-shaped, red-fleshed fruit that is eaten fresh in Brazil, while the whole plant has long served as emergency fodder for livestock during drought in its native region. It is more cold-sensitive than South American Cereus species like C. hildmannianus and should be protected whenever temperatures approach freezing, making it best suited to large containers in regions outside the warmest zones.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online
Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Let a cut section callus for one to two weeks in a dry, shaded spot, then set the base into very well-drained, sandy soil in full sun in spring; as a named cultivar it must be propagated from cuttings to retain its spiraled ribs.

directions: Plant a callused cutting in very well-drained, sandy soil in full sun. This striking columnar cactus cultivar is grown for its ribs, which twist in a tight spiral up the stem rather than running straight, giving the whole plant a dramatic corkscrew silhouette that is popular as a container and landscape accent in frost-free regions. Like other Cereus, it produces large white nocturnal flowers on mature stems and grows relatively quickly once established. The cultivar's precise species parentage is debated among growers, with plants sold under this name variously labeled Cereus forbesii, Cereus validus, or Cereus tetragonus 'Spiralis'; buy from a reputable succulent nursery and expect some variation in mature spiral tightness between sources.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow in a shallow pot in bright light with fast-draining, gritty cactus mix; native to pine-oak highlands rather than low desert, it appreciates slightly more moisture and part shade than most Mammillaria species.

directions: Grow in a shallow pot or rock garden pocket in bright light with fast-draining, gritty soil. Native to high-elevation pine-oak forest in Chihuahua, Mexico, this clustering cactus carries dense, soft, golden to white bristly spines that give it a shaggy 'old man' appearance, and in spring it produces unusually large, vivid red to orange-red flowers relative to its small stem size. Because it grows naturally in a cooler, slightly moister mountain habitat than most desert Mammillaria, it is somewhat less drought-tolerant and benefits from a touch more shade and humidity than typical low-desert pincushion cacti, making it a good candidate for a protected, part-shade container spot. Water only when the soil has dried and separate rooted offsets to propagate a clump.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow in a shallow pot or rock garden pocket in bright light with fast-draining, gritty cactus mix; a distinct cool, dry winter rest encourages the heaviest spring flowering.

directions: Grow in a shallow pot or rock garden pocket in bright light with fast-draining, gritty soil. Native to the central Mexican highlands, this small, clustering, globular cactus is densely covered in fine, soft, pure white hair-like spines that nearly hide the green stem beneath, creating a snowball-like effect. Small, pale cream to pale pink flowers form a ring near the crown in spring, followed by slender pink to red fruit. It offsets readily from the base over a few years to form a tight mound of small white heads, making it a good candidate for a dish garden alongside other small Mexican Mammillaria species.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow in a shallow pot in bright light with fast-draining, gritty cactus mix; this narrow Hidalgo endemic is slower and somewhat more demanding in cultivation than common nursery Mammillaria species.

directions: Grow in a shallow pot in bright light with fast-draining, gritty soil. Native to a narrow area of Hidalgo, Mexico, this clustering cactus is densely clothed in fine, soft, white, feathery spines that completely obscure the stems beneath, forming tight mounds of woolly-looking heads that give rise to its 'old lady' nickname. Small pink flowers appear in a ring near the crown in spring on mature clusters. It is slower-growing and somewhat less tolerant of overwatering than more commonly cultivated Mammillaria species, so err on the side of underwatering and provide excellent drainage and strong light to keep the spine covering dense and white.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Let a cut offset callus for several days, then set it into very well-drained, sandy soil in full sun in spring; established clumps spread widely and flower most heavily in their second year and beyond.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, sandy soil in full sun. Native to scrubland in central Argentina, this sprawling, clustering cactus sends up thick, blue-green, ribbed stems armed with yellowish-brown spines that lean and pile together to form a wide, low mound over time. In late spring and early summer it produces some of the largest flowers in the genus: enormous, fragrant, white trumpets up to 10 inches across that open in the evening and persist into the following morning. It spreads readily from rooted stem cuttings or offsets and tolerates occasional light frost once established, though hard freezes will damage or kill exposed stems.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

common_name: Orange Easter Lily Cactus (Huascha Torch Cactus)

planting.note: Let a cut offset callus for several days, then set it into very well-drained, sandy soil in full sun in spring; unlike many white-flowered Echinopsis, this species blooms by day rather than only at night.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, sandy soil in full sun. Native to arid Andean foothills of northwestern Argentina, this clustering, semi-sprawling cactus produces slender, ribbed, blue-green stems that branch from the base over time. It stands out among Echinopsis relatives for its day-opening, trumpet-shaped flowers, most commonly a vivid orange-red though yellow-flowered forms also occur in habitat and cultivation, appearing over several weeks in late spring and summer. It offsets freely and is propagated from rooted stem cuttings; give it the same lean, sharply drained soil and full sun as other Echinopsis and protect from hard freezes.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference
